How to use Visual Studio Code

html:
Welcome

This is a 30 days of Python programming challenge. In this challenge, you will learn everything you need to be a Python programmer and the whole concept of programming. At the end of the challenge you will get a 30DaysOfPython programming challenge certificate.

If you would like to actively engage in the challenge, you may join the 30DaysOfPython challenge telegram group.

Introduction

This section is your first look at Python itself: what the language is, what people actually use it for, why it became the main language of AI, and which fields hire Python programmers the most. After that, Day 1 continues with setup, the Python shell, and your first lines of code.

This 30 days of Python challenge will help you learn the latest version of Python, Python 3, step by step. The topics are broken down into 30 days. Each day contains several topics with easy-to-understand explanations, real-world examples, and many hands-on exercises and projects.

This challenge is designed for beginners and professionals who want to learn the Python programming language. It may take 30 to 100 days to complete. People who actively participate in the telegram group have a high probability of completing the challenge.

This challenge is easy to read, written in conversational English, engaging, motivating and at the same time very demanding. You need to allocate enough time to finish it. If you are a visual learner, you may get the video lesson on the <a href="https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC7PNRuno1rzYPb1xLa4yktw">Washera</a> YouTube channel. You may start from Python for Absolute Beginners video. Subscribe to the channel, comment and ask questions on YouTube videos and be proactive.

What is Python?

Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language. High-level means you write instructions that look close to English instead of talking to the computer in ones and zeros. General-purpose means the same language can build a website, analyze a spreadsheet, automate a boring office task, or train an AI model.

A few facts that help you place it:

  • Created by Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer.
  • First released on 20 February 1991.
  • Named after the British comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake.
  • Open source: anyone can use it, read it, and contribute to it for free.
  • Interpreted: Python runs your code line by line. You do not compile it into a separate program first.
  • Object-oriented: you can group data and behavior into objects (you will meet this idea later in the challenge).
  • Dynamically typed: you do not have to declare a variable's type before you use it.

Python's design goal is readability. Compare a simple print in Python with the same idea in a more verbose language: you write print('Hello, World!') and you are done. That short path from idea to working code is why beginners start here and why professionals stay here.

The version you will learn in this challenge is Python 3.

How Python is used

Think of Python as a toolkit, not a single job title. People use it to:

  1. Write programs and scripts — from a five-line file that renames photos to a large application used by millions of people.
  2. Automate work — move files, send emails, fill reports, scrape websites, and connect one tool to another.
  3. Build web applications and APIs — with frameworks such as Django, Flask, and FastAPI.
  4. Work with data — clean tables, plot charts, run statistics, and prepare datasets.
  5. Build AI and machine learning systems — train models, run predictions, and talk to large language models.
  6. Control hardware and science experiments — from Raspberry Pi projects to lab instruments.
  7. Teach programming — many universities and bootcamps start with Python because the syntax stays out of the way.

You will not do all of that on Day 1. You only need the picture: one language, many doors.

Python for Artificial Intelligence

Python is the most common language in AI and machine learning. That is not because it is the fastest language on the CPU. It is because the AI community built almost all of its shared tools in Python, and because the language is easy to experiment with.

Here is what "Python for AI" actually means in practice:

  • Data first. AI models learn from data. Python (with libraries such as NumPy and pandas) is how people load, clean, and explore that data.
  • Model training. Libraries such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch let you train models for prediction, classification, computer vision, and language.
  • Deep learning and large language models. Modern AI — image generators, chatbots, speech systems — is usually trained and served with Python code.
  • Glue code. Researchers and engineers use Python to connect data, models, APIs, and user interfaces. A short Python script can call an AI API and print the answer.
  • Notebooks. Tools such as Jupyter let you mix explanation, code, and charts. That workflow is standard in AI work.

If your goal is AI, this 30-day challenge is still the right start. AI libraries sit on top of the same basics you learn here: variables, lists, loops, functions, files, and packages. Without those, the AI tools will feel like magic you cannot control.

Fields where Python is mostly used

Python shows up in many industries. These are the fields where it is used the most:

Field What people use Python for
Artificial intelligence and machine learning Training models, computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation systems
Data science and analytics Cleaning data, statistics, dashboards, business reports
Web development Websites, backends, REST APIs
Automation and scripting Everyday tasks, DevOps, testing, system administration
Scientific computing and research Physics, biology, chemistry, astronomy, simulations
Finance and fintech Trading tools, risk models, data pipelines
Cybersecurity Scanning, log analysis, small security tools
Education Teaching programming and computational thinking
Game tooling and desktop apps Tools around games, simple desktop programs, Raspberry Pi projects
Software testing and quality Test automation and quality scripts

Companies that use Python include Google, Netflix, Instagram, Spotify, NASA, and many banks, hospitals, and startups. You do not need to pick a field today. Learn the language first. The field comes later.

Why Python

Python is close to human language, so it is easier to learn and use than many older languages. You can read a simple Python program even before you know every keyword.

It is used by many industries and companies, including Google. People build web apps, desktop tools, system-administration scripts, data pipelines, and machine-learning libraries with it. The data science and AI community in particular has made Python its default language.

I hope this is enough to convince you to start. Python is eating the world and you are killing it before it eats you.

Environment Setup

Installing Python

To run a Python script you need to install Python. Download it from python.org.

Windows

  1. Open https://www.python.org/.
  2. Open Downloads, then Windows. The page title is Python Releases for Windows.
  3. Click Latest Python 3 Release. The download page used to show Python 3.8.0 next to a Python 2.7.17 line. Use the current Python 3 release. Do not install Python 2.
  4. Run the installer. Tick Add python.exe to PATH, then choose Install Now.

macOS

  1. Open https://www.python.org/.
  2. Open Downloads. The menu lists All releases, Source code, Windows, Mac OS X, Other Platforms, License.
  3. Under Download for Mac OS X, click the Python 3 button (the page used to show Python 3.8.0).
  4. The page also says Python can be used on many operating systems. Use View the full list of downloads if you are not on Mac.
  5. Run the .pkg installer.

Check the version

Open your terminal (macOS / Linux) or Command Prompt / PowerShell (Windows) and run one of these:

terminal
python --version
terminal
python3 --version

On some machines the command is python. On others it is python3. Use the one that prints a version.

View (example from an older install; yours will be a later 3.x):

output.txt
Python 3.7.5

Your version of Python might be different. It should be 3.6 or above. If you see a Python 3 version, Python is installed. Continue to the next section.

Python Shell

Python is an interpreted scripting language, so it does not need to be compiled. It executes the code line by line. Python comes with a Python Shell (Python Interactive Shell). It is used to execute a single Python command and get the result.

The Python shell waits for code from you. When you enter a line, it interprets that line and shows the result on the next line.

1. Open the shell

Open your terminal or command prompt and write:

terminal
python

View:

output.txt
Python 3.7.5 (default, Nov  1 2019, 02:16:32)
[Clang 11.0.0 (clang-1100.0.33.8)] on darwin
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>>

The >>> prompt means the shell is waiting. Type Python next to >>> and press Enter.

2. First expression

This is the first script on the Python interactive shell:

example.py
10 + 20

View:

output.txt
>>> 10 + 20
30
>>>

You wrote your first Python script on the interactive shell.

3. Exit the shell

To close the shell, next to >>> write exit() and press Enter.

example.py
exit()

View:

output.txt
>>> 10 + 20
30
>>> exit()

After exit() you are back in the normal terminal. You now know how to open the Python interactive shell and how to leave it.

4. Syntax errors

Python gives you a result if it understands the script. If not, it returns an error. Make a deliberate mistake and see what Python returns.

example.py
10 + 20
10 x 20

View:

output.txt
>>> 10 + 20
30
>>> 10 x 20
  File "<stdin>", line 1
    10 x 20
       ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax

Using x as multiplication is a syntax error. x is not a valid operator in Python. Use an asterisk (*) for multiplication. The error points at the character to fix.

The process of identifying and removing errors from a program is called debugging.

5. Debugging

Debug the line by putting * in place of x.

example.py
10 + 20
10 x 20
10 * 20

View:

output.txt
>>> 10 + 20
30
>>> 10 x 20
  File "<stdin>", line 1
    10 x 20
       ^
SyntaxError: invalid syntax
>>> 10 * 20
200

The bug is fixed. The code ran and we got the result we expected. As a programmer you will see this kind of error on a daily basis. It is good to know how to debug. To be good at debugging you should understand what kind of error you are facing. Some of the Python errors you may encounter are SyntaxError, IndexError, NameError, ModuleNotFoundError, KeyError, ImportError, AttributeError, TypeError, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError. We will see more about different Python error types in later sections.

6. Comments

A comment is a part of the code which is not executed by Python. Leave text in the code to make it more readable. Python does not run the comment. A comment starts with a hash (#) symbol.

example.py
# comment starts with hash
# this is a python comment, because it starts with a (#) symbol

In the interactive shell a comment-only line shows ... and no result.

example.py
# This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step

View:

output.txt
>>> # This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step
...

7. Arithmetic on the shell

Practice the Python interactive shell. Open it again with python. Do basic mathematical operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulus, exponentiation).

Do the maths on paper first, then type the same expressions as Python code. The structured numbers today are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50.

  • 10 + 20 = 30
  • 30 - 10 = 20
  • 10 * 20 = 200
  • 30 / 10 = 3.0
  • 10 ** 2 = 10 x 10 = 100

In Python we also have:

  • 30 % 20 = 10 => remainder
  • 30 // 20 = 1 => remove the remainder (floor division)
# Operator Name Example View
1 + Addition 10 + 20 30
2 - Subtraction 30 - 10 20
3 * Multiplication (not x) 10 * 20 200
4 / Division 30 / 10 3.0
5 % Modulus (remainder) 30 % 20 10
6 % Modulus when the left number is smaller 20 % 30 20
7 // Floor division 30 // 20 1
8 ** Exponent 10 ** 2 100

Same session written as code. Comments sit on the same line as the expression.

example.py
# This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step
10 + 20     # addition(+)
30 - 10     # subtraction(-)
10 * 20     # multiplication(*) not x
30 / 10     # division(/)
30 % 20     # modulus(%) - finding the remainder
20 % 30     # modulus(%) - finding the remainder
# Why is the value above 20?
30 // 20    # floor division operator(//) - it removes the remainder
10 ** 2     # exponential operator(**) - equivalent to 10^2 = 10 * 10
# Well done. Now you know how to use the Python interactive shell

View:

output.txt
>>> # This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step
...
>>> 10 + 20     # addition(+)
30
>>> 30 - 10     # subtraction(-)
20
>>> 10 * 20     # multiplication(*) not x
200
>>> 30 / 10     # division(/)
3.0
>>> 30 % 20     # modulus(%) - finding the remainder
10
>>> 20 % 30     # modulus(%) - finding the remainder
20
>>> # Why is the value above 20?
...
>>> 30 // 20    # floor division operator(//) - it removes the remainder
1
>>> 10 ** 2     # exponential operator(**) - equivalent to 10^2 = 10 * 10
100
>>> # Well done. Now you know how to use the Python interactive shell
...

20 % 30 is 20 because 20 is smaller than 30. Python can take zero groups of 30 out of 20, so the remainder is the whole 20.

8. Strings on the shell

Close the opened shell with exit() and open it again. Practice writing text. Any text in quotes is a string. Use a single quote or a double quote. Use a triple quote if the text is more than one line.

example.py
# Let's practice how to write text on the Python shell.
# We use a single or double quote to make a string.
'Priya'          # name as a string, single quotes
"Priya"          # same name, double quotes
# A string can be one character or a whole page
'I love teaching. And thank you so much for joining this course'
# If the text is too long we use a triple quote
'''We use triple quote if the text is more than one line'''
# Now you know strings and how to use the Python shell
# Next we install a text editor / code editor
exit()

View:

output.txt
>>> 'Priya'          # name as a string, single quotes
'Priya'
>>> "Priya"          # same name, double quotes
'Priya'
>>> # A string can be one character or a whole page
...
>>> 'I love teaching. And thank you so much for joining this course'
'I love teaching. And thank you so much for joining this course'
>>> # If the text is too long we use a triple quote
...
>>> '''We use triple quote if the text is more than one line'''
'We use triple quote if the text is more than one line'
>>> exit()

Single quotes and double quotes print the same string. The shell shows strings with single quotes.

Installing Visual Studio Code

The Python interactive shell is good to try and test small script codes but it will not be for a big project. In a real work environment, developers use different code editors to write codes. In this 30 days of Python programming challenge, we will use Visual Studio Code. Visual Studio Code is a very popular open source text editor. Download it from https://code.visualstudio.com/. If you prefer another editor, follow along with what you have.

Download steps (from the Visual Studio Code site)

  1. Open https://code.visualstudio.com/.
  2. The page title is Code editing. Redefined. It is free and open source.
  3. Use the big download button for your system, or the table:
System Installer
macOS Package (Stable or Insiders)
Windows x64 User Installer (Stable or Insiders)
Linux x64 .deb or .rpm (Stable or Insiders)
  1. Use Other downloads if your system is not in that table.
  2. Run the installer.

If you prefer a video, you can follow this Visual Studio Code for Python video tutorial.

How to use Visual Studio Code

Open Visual Studio Code by double-clicking its icon. The first window is a Welcome page plus the Explorer.

What you see

  1. Activity bar (far left). Top icon is Explorer (two documents). Below it: Search, Source Control, Run and Debug, Extensions, then Account and Settings at the bottom.
  2. Explorer panel. It shows OPEN EDITORS and NO FOLDER OPENED until you add a folder.
  3. Add Folder / Open Folder button in that panel.
  4. Welcome tab in the editor:
    • Open folder... / Add workspace folder...
    • Recent projects (example list: 30DaysOfPython, git-lesson, portfolio-react)
    • Help links (keyboard cheatsheet, introductory videos, tips, docs)
    • Tools and languages, Settings and keybindings, Color theme
    • Learn: find commands, interface overview, interactive playground
  5. Checkbox Show welcome page on startup at the bottom of Welcome.
  6. Status bar at the very bottom (errors, warnings, account, Live Share).

Open the project folder

  1. Create a folder named 30DaysOfPython on your desktop.
  2. In Explorer, click Open Folder. The empty state says You have not yet opened a folder.
  3. In the file dialog, go to Desktop and select the 30DaysOfPython folder.
  4. Click Open. (The dialog also has Cancel and New Folder.)

Create the first file

After the folder is open, Explorer shows shortcuts on the 30DAYSOF... row:

  1. Click the New File icon (page with a plus) to create a file.
  2. Click the New Folder icon (folder with a plus) to create a folder.
  3. Name the file helloworld.py. A Python file always uses the .py extension.
  4. Click the Explorer icon on the activity bar to show or hide the file tree.

Close the opened project

  1. Right-click the 30DaysOfPython folder name in Explorer (not the file).
  2. The menu includes: New File, New Folder, Reveal in Finder, Open in Terminal, Add Folder to Workspace, Open Folder Settings, Remove Folder from Workspace, Find in Folder, Paste, Copy Path, Copy Relative Path, Generate .editorconfig, Deploy to Web App.
  3. Choose Remove Folder from Workspace.

The development environment is ready. Next we write Python.

Basic Python

Python Syntax

A Python script can be written in the Python interactive shell or in the code editor. A Python file has an extension .py.

Python Indentation

An indentation is a white space in a text. Indentation in many languages is used to increase code readability; however, Python uses indentation to create blocks of code. In other programming languages, curly brackets are used to create code blocks instead of indentation. One of the common bugs when writing Python code is incorrect indentation.

A line that starts with extra space before any block is an error.

example.py
    "Hello, World!"    # This will cause an indentation error
"Hello, World!"        # This will run without causing error

View:

output.txt
>>>     "Hello, World!"    # This will cause an indentation error
  File "<stdin>", line 1
    "Hello, World!"    # This will cause an indentation error
IndentationError: unexpected indent
>>> "Hello, World!"        # This will run without causing error
'Hello, World!'

Do not put spaces in front of a top-level line. You will use indentation on purpose later, inside if and loops.

Comments

Comments play a crucial role in enhancing code readability and allowing developers to leave notes within their code. In Python, any text preceded by a hash (#) symbol is considered a comment and is not executed when the code runs.

Example: Single Line Comment

example.py
# This is the first comment
# This is the second comment
# Python is eating the world

Example: Multiline Comment

A triple quote can be used for a multiline comment if it is not assigned to a variable.

example.py
"""This is multiline comment
multiline comment takes multiple lines.
python is eating the world
"""

Data types

In Python there are several types of data types. Let us get started with the most common ones. Different data types will be covered in detail in other sections. For the time being, let us just go through the different data types and get familiar with them. You do not have to have a clear understanding now.

Number

  • Integer: Integer (negative, zero and positive) numbers Example: ... -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 ... Structured set we use today: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
  • Float: Decimal number Example: ... -3.5, -2.25, -1.0, 0.0, 1.1, 2.2, 3.5 ... Structured examples: 10.0, 3.14, 9.81
  • Complex Example: 1 + 1j, 2 + 4j Structured example: 1 + 3j

String

A collection of one or more characters under a single or double quote. If a string is more than one sentence then we use a triple quote.

Example:

example.py
'Priya'
'India'
'Python'
'I love teaching'
'I hope you are enjoying the first day of 30DaysOfPython Challenge'

Booleans

A boolean data type is either a True or False value. T and F should be always uppercase.

Example:

example.py
True   # Is the light on? If it is on, then the value is True
False  # Is the light on? If it is off, then the value is False

List

Python list is an ordered collection which allows to store different data type items. A list is similar to an array in JavaScript.

Example:

example.py
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]                 # all the same data types - a list of numbers
['Banana', 'Orange', 'Mango', 'Avocado']  # all the same data types - a list of strings (fruits)
['India', 'Finland', 'Sweden', 'Norway']  # all the same data types - a list of strings (countries)
['Banana', 10, False, 9.81]          # different data types - string, integer, boolean and float

Dictionary

A Python dictionary object is an unordered collection of data in a key value pair format.

Example:

example.py
{
    'first_name': 'Priya',
    'last_name': 'Rao',
    'country': 'India',
    'city': 'Hyderabad',
    'age': 22,
    'is_married': False,
    'skills': ['JS', 'React', 'Node', 'Python']
}

Tuple

A tuple is an ordered collection of different data types like list but tuples can not be modified once they are created. They are immutable.

Example:

example.py
('Priya', 'Rao', 'Brook', 'Abraham', 'Lidiya')  # Names
example.py
('Earth', 'Jupiter', 'Neptune', 'Mars', 'Venus', 'Saturn', 'Uranus', 'Mercury')  # planets

Set

A set is a collection of data types similar to list and tuple. Unlike list and tuple, set is not an ordered collection of items. Like in Mathematics, set in Python stores only unique items.

In later sections, we will go in detail about each and every Python data type.

Example:

example.py
{10, 20, 30, 40}
{3.14, 9.81, 2.7}  # order is not important in set

Checking Data types

To check the data type of certain data/variable we use the type function.

example.py
type(10)
type(3.14)
type(1 + 3j)
type('Priya')
type([10, 20, 30])
type({'name': 'Priya'})
type((10, 20, 30, 40))
type({9.8, 3.14, 2.7})
exit()

View:

output.txt
>>> type(10)
<class 'int'>
>>> type(3.14)
<class 'float'>
>>> type(1 + 3j)
<class 'complex'>
>>> type('Priya')
<class 'str'>
>>> type([10, 20, 30])
<class 'list'>
>>> type({'name': 'Priya'})
<class 'dict'>
>>> type((10, 20, 30, 40))
<class 'tuple'>
>>> type({9.8, 3.14, 2.7})
<class 'set'>
>>> exit()
# Value type() view
1 10 <class 'int'>
2 3.14 <class 'float'>
3 1 + 3j <class 'complex'>
4 'Priya' <class 'str'>
5 [10, 20, 30] <class 'list'>
6 {'name': 'Priya'} <class 'dict'>
7 (10, 20, 30, 40) <class 'tuple'>
8 {9.8, 3.14, 2.7} <class 'set'>

Python File

First open your project folder, 30DaysOfPython. If you don't have this folder, create a folder named 30DaysOfPython. Inside this folder, create a file called helloworld.py. Now, let's do what we did on the Python interactive shell using Visual Studio Code.

The Python interactive shell was printing without using print. In a .py file you must use the built-in function print() to see a result. print() takes one or more arguments: print('argument1', 'argument2', 'argument3').

Example

The file name is helloworld.py.

example.py
# Day 1 - 30DaysOfPython Challenge

print('Hello, World!')

print(10 + 20)             # addition(+)
print(30 - 10)             # subtraction(-)
print(10 * 20)             # multiplication(*)
print(30 / 10)             # division(/)
print(10 ** 2)             # exponential(**)
print(30 % 20)             # modulus(%)
print(30 // 20)            # Floor division operator(//)

# Checking data types
print(type(10))                  # Int
print(type(3.14))                # Float
print(type(1 + 3j))              # Complex
print(type('Priya'))             # String
print(type([10, 20, 30]))        # List
print(type({'name': 'Priya'}))   # Dictionary
print(type({10, 20, 30}))        # Set
print(type((10, 20, 30)))        # Tuple

How to run it

  1. Open helloworld.py in the Explorer (it sits under the 30DaysOfPython folder).
  2. Click the green Run triangle at the top right of the editor, or
  3. Open the Terminal panel and type:
terminal
python helloworld.py

View:

output.txt
Hello, World!
30
20
200
3.0
100
10
1
<class 'int'>
<class 'float'>
<class 'complex'>
<class 'str'>
<class 'list'>
<class 'dict'>
<class 'set'>
<class 'tuple'>

You finished the Day 1 lesson. Practice with the exercises below.

Exercises

Exercises: Level 1

  1. Check the python version you are using
  2. Open the python interactive shell and do the following operations. The operands are 3 and 4.
    • addition(+)
    • subtraction(-)
    • multiplication(*)
    • modulus(%)
    • division(/)
    • exponential(**)
    • floor division operator(//)
  3. Write strings on the python interactive shell. The strings are the following:
    • Your name
    • Your family name
    • Your country
    • I am enjoying 30 days of python
  4. Check the data types of the following data:
    • 10
    • 9.8
    • 3.14
    • 4 - 4j
    • ['Asabeneh', 'Python', 'Finland']
    • Your name
    • Your family name
    • Your country

Exercises: Level 2

  1. Create a folder named day_1 inside 30DaysOfPython folder. Inside day_1 folder, create a python file helloworld.py and repeat questions 1, 2, 3 and 4. Remember to use print() when you are working on a python file. Navigate to the directory where you have saved your file, and run it.

Exercises: Level 3

  1. Write an example for different Python data types such as Number(Integer, Float, Complex), String, Boolean, List, Tuple, Set and Dictionary.
  2. Find an Euclidean distance between (2, 3) and (10, 8)
  3. Store the structured numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in a list named scores. Use print(scores) and print(type(scores))
  4. Use print() and type() on 10, 20.0, 10 + 20j, 'Priya', and True. Print each value and each type
  5. Print each score with a label: print('score 1:', 10) through print('score 5:', 50)
  6. Print 10 + 20, 30 - 10, 10 * 20, 30 / 10, 10 ** 2, 30 % 20, and 30 // 20. Then print type() of each result
  7. Build a dictionary for Priya Rao in Hyderabad, India, with a score of 20. Print the dictionary and type() of it
  8. Compare type([10, 20, 30]), type((10, 20, 30)), and type({10, 20, 30}). Print all three views and write one comment about the difference

You finished Day 1. Next: variables and built-in functions.

A few facts that help you place it: Created by Guido van Rossum, a Dutch programmer. First released on 20 February 1991. Named after the British comedy series Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake. Open source: anyone can use it, read it, and contribute to it for free. Interpreted: Python runs your code line by line. You do not compile it into a separate program first. Object-oriented: you can group data and behavior into objects (you will meet this idea later in the challenge). Dynamically typed: you do not have to declare a variable's type before you use it. Python's design goal is readability. Compare a simple print in Python with the same idea in a more verbose language: you write print('Hello, World!') and you are done. That short path from idea to working code is why beginners start here and why professionals stay here. The version you will learn in this challenge is Python 3. How Python is used Think of Python as a toolkit, not a single job title. People use it to: Write programs and scripts — from a five-line file that renames photos to a large application used by millions of people. Automate work — move files, send emails, fill reports, scrape websites, and connect one tool to another. Build web applications and APIs — with frameworks such as Django, Flask, and FastAPI. Work with data — clean tables, plot charts, run statistics, and prepare datasets. Build AI and machine learning systems — train models, run predictions, and talk to large language models. Control hardware and science experiments — from Raspberry Pi projects to lab instruments. Teach programming — many universities and bootcamps start with Python because the syntax stays out of the way. You will not do all of that on Day 1. You only need the picture: one language, many doors. Python for Artificial Intelligence Python is the most common language in AI and machine learning. That is not because it is the fastest language on the CPU. It is because the AI community built almost all of its shared tools in Python, and because the language is easy to experiment with. Here is what "Python for AI" actually means in practice: Data first. AI models learn from data. Python (with libraries such as NumPy and pandas) is how people load, clean, and explore that data. Model training. Libraries such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and PyTorch let you train models for prediction, classification, computer vision, and language. Deep learning and large language models. Modern AI — image generators, chatbots, speech systems — is usually trained and served with Python code. Glue code. Researchers and engineers use Python to connect data, models, APIs, and user interfaces. A short Python script can call an AI API and print the answer. Notebooks. Tools such as Jupyter let you mix explanation, code, and charts. That workflow is standard in AI work. If your goal is AI, this 30-day challenge is still the right start. AI libraries sit on top of the same basics you learn here: variables, lists, loops, functions, files, and packages. Without those, the AI tools will feel like magic you cannot control. Fields where Python is mostly used Python shows up in many industries. These are the fields where it is used the most: Field What people use Python for Artificial intelligence and machine learning Training models, computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation systems Data science and analytics Cleaning data, statistics, dashboards, business reports Web development Websites, backends, REST APIs Automation and scripting Everyday tasks, DevOps, testing, system administration Scientific computing and research Physics, biology, chemistry, astronomy, simulations Finance and fintech Trading tools, risk models, data pipelines Cybersecurity Scanning, log analysis, small security tools Education Teaching programming and computational thinking Game tooling and desktop apps Tools around games, simple desktop programs, Raspberry Pi projects Software testing and quality Test automation and quality scripts Companies that use Python include Google, Netflix, Instagram, Spotify, NASA, and many banks, hospitals, and startups. You do not need to pick a field today. Learn the language first. The field comes later. Why Python Python is close to human language, so it is easier to learn and use than many older languages. You can read a simple Python program even before you know every keyword. It is used by many industries and companies, including Google. People build web apps, desktop tools, system-administration scripts, data pipelines, and machine-learning libraries with it. The data science and AI community in particular has made Python its default language. I hope this is enough to convince you to start. Python is eating the world and you are killing it before it eats you. Environment Setup Installing Python To run a Python script you need to install Python. Download it from python.org. Windows Open https://www.python.org/. Open Downloads, then Windows. The page title is Python Releases for Windows. Click Latest Python 3 Release. The download page used to show Python 3.8.0 next to a Python 2.7.17 line. Use the current Python 3 release. Do not install Python 2. Run the installer. Tick Add python.exe to PATH, then choose Install Now. macOS Open https://www.python.org/. Open Downloads. The menu lists All releases, Source code, Windows, Mac OS X, Other Platforms, License. Under Download for Mac OS X, click the Python 3 button (the page used to show Python 3.8.0). The page also says Python can be used on many operating systems. Use View the full list of downloads if you are not on Mac. Run the .pkg installer. Check the version Open your terminal (macOS / Linux) or Command Prompt / PowerShell (Windows) and run one of these: terminal python --version terminal python3 --version On some machines the command is python. On others it is python3. Use the one that prints a version. View (example from an older install; yours will be a later 3.x): output.txt Python 3.7.5 Your version of Python might be different. It should be 3.6 or above. If you see a Python 3 version, Python is installed. Continue to the next section. Python Shell Python is an interpreted scripting language, so it does not need to be compiled. It executes the code line by line. Python comes with a Python Shell (Python Interactive Shell). It is used to execute a single Python command and get the result. The Python shell waits for code from you. When you enter a line, it interprets that line and shows the result on the next line. 1. Open the shell Open your terminal or command prompt and write: terminal python View: output.txt Python 3.7.5 (default, Nov 1 2019, 02:16:32) [Clang 11.0.0 (clang-1100.0.33.8)] on darwin Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information. >>> The >>> prompt means the shell is waiting. Type Python next to >>> and press Enter. 2. First expression This is the first script on the Python interactive shell: example.py 10 + 20 View: output.txt >>> 10 + 20 30 >>> You wrote your first Python script on the interactive shell. 3. Exit the shell To close the shell, next to >>> write exit() and press Enter. example.py exit() View: output.txt >>> 10 + 20 30 >>> exit() After exit() you are back in the normal terminal. You now know how to open the Python interactive shell and how to leave it. 4. Syntax errors Python gives you a result if it understands the script. If not, it returns an error. Make a deliberate mistake and see what Python returns. example.py 10 + 20 10 x 20 View: output.txt >>> 10 + 20 30 >>> 10 x 20 File "", line 1 10 x 20 ^ SyntaxError: invalid syntax Using x as multiplication is a syntax error. x is not a valid operator in Python. Use an asterisk (*) for multiplication. The error points at the character to fix. The process of identifying and removing errors from a program is called debugging. 5. Debugging Debug the line by putting * in place of x. example.py 10 + 20 10 x 20 10 * 20 View: output.txt >>> 10 + 20 30 >>> 10 x 20 File "", line 1 10 x 20 ^ SyntaxError: invalid syntax >>> 10 * 20 200 The bug is fixed. The code ran and we got the result we expected. As a programmer you will see this kind of error on a daily basis. It is good to know how to debug. To be good at debugging you should understand what kind of error you are facing. Some of the Python errors you may encounter are SyntaxError, IndexError, NameError, ModuleNotFoundError, KeyError, ImportError, AttributeError, TypeError, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError. We will see more about different Python error types in later sections. 6. Comments A comment is a part of the code which is not executed by Python. Leave text in the code to make it more readable. Python does not run the comment. A comment starts with a hash (#) symbol. example.py # comment starts with hash # this is a python comment, because it starts with a (#) symbol In the interactive shell a comment-only line shows ... and no result. example.py # This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step View: output.txt >>> # This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step ... 7. Arithmetic on the shell Practice the Python interactive shell. Open it again with python. Do basic mathematical operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, modulus, exponentiation). Do the maths on paper first, then type the same expressions as Python code. The structured numbers today are 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. 10 + 20 = 30 30 - 10 = 20 10 * 20 = 200 30 / 10 = 3.0 10 ** 2 = 10 x 10 = 100 In Python we also have: 30 % 20 = 10 => remainder 30 // 20 = 1 => remove the remainder (floor division) # Operator Name Example View 1 + Addition 10 + 20 30 2 - Subtraction 30 - 10 20 3 * Multiplication (not x) 10 * 20 200 4 / Division 30 / 10 3.0 5 % Modulus (remainder) 30 % 20 10 6 % Modulus when the left number is smaller 20 % 30 20 7 // Floor division 30 // 20 1 8 ** Exponent 10 ** 2 100 Same session written as code. Comments sit on the same line as the expression. example.py # This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step 10 + 20 # addition(+) 30 - 10 # subtraction(-) 10 * 20 # multiplication(*) not x 30 / 10 # division(/) 30 % 20 # modulus(%) - finding the remainder 20 % 30 # modulus(%) - finding the remainder # Why is the value above 20? 30 // 20 # floor division operator(//) - it removes the remainder 10 ** 2 # exponential operator(**) - equivalent to 10^2 = 10 * 10 # Well done. Now you know how to use the Python interactive shell View: output.txt >>> # This is my first Python comment. Do everything step by step ... >>> 10 + 20 # addition(+) 30 >>> 30 - 10 # subtraction(-) 20 >>> 10 * 20 # multiplication(*) not x 200 >>> 30 / 10 # division(/) 3.0 >>> 30 % 20 # modulus(%) - finding the remainder 10 >>> 20 % 30 # modulus(%) - finding the remainder 20 >>> # Why is the value above 20? ... >>> 30 // 20 # floor division operator(//) - it removes the remainder 1 >>> 10 ** 2 # exponential operator(**) - equivalent to 10^2 = 10 * 10 100 >>> # Well done. Now you know how to use the Python interactive shell ... 20 % 30 is 20 because 20 is smaller than 30. Python can take zero groups of 30 out of 20, so the remainder is the whole 20. 8. Strings on the shell Close the opened shell with exit() and open it again. Practice writing text. Any text in quotes is a string. Use a single quote or a double quote. Use a triple quote if the text is more than one line. example.py # Let's practice how to write text on the Python shell. # We use a single or double quote to make a string. 'Priya' # name as a string, single quotes "Priya" # same name, double quotes # A string can be one character or a whole page 'I love teaching. And thank you so much for joining this course' # If the text is too long we use a triple quote '''We use triple quote if the text is more than one line''' # Now you know strings and how to use the Python shell # Next we install a text editor / code editor exit() View: output.txt >>> 'Priya' # name as a string, single quotes 'Priya' >>> "Priya" # same name, double quotes 'Priya' >>> # A string can be one character or a whole page ... >>> 'I love teaching. And thank you so much for joining this course' 'I love teaching. And thank you so much for joining this course' >>> # If the text is too long we use a triple quote ... >>> '''We use triple quote if the text is more than one line''' 'We use triple quote if the text is more than one line' >>> exit() Single quotes and double quotes print the same string. The shell shows strings with single quotes. Installing Visual Studio Code The Python interactive shell is good to try and test small script codes but it will not be for a big project. In a real work environment, developers use different code editors to write codes. In this 30 days of Python programming challenge, we will use Visual Studio Code. Visual Studio Code is a very popular open source text editor. Download it from https://code.visualstudio.com/. If you prefer another editor, follow along with what you have. Download steps (from the Visual Studio Code site) Open https://code.visualstudio.com/. The page title is Code editing. Redefined. It is free and open source. Use the big download button for your system, or the table: System Installer macOS Package (Stable or Insiders) Windows x64 User Installer (Stable or Insiders) Linux x64 .deb or .rpm (Stable or Insiders) Use Other downloads if your system is not in that table. Run the installer. If you prefer a video, you can follow this Visual Studio Code for Python video tutorial. How to use Visual Studio Code Open Visual Studio Code by double-clicking its icon. The first window is a Welcome page plus the Explorer. What you see Activity bar (far left). Top icon is Explorer (two documents). Below it: Search, Source Control, Run and Debug, Extensions, then Account and Settings at the bottom. Explorer panel. It shows OPEN EDITORS and NO FOLDER OPENED until you add a folder. Add Folder / Open Folder button in that panel. Welcome tab in the editor: Open folder... / Add workspace folder... Recent projects (example list: 30DaysOfPython, git-lesson, portfolio-react) Help links (keyboard cheatsheet, introductory videos, tips, docs) Tools and languages, Settings and keybindings, Color theme Learn: find commands, interface overview, interactive playground Checkbox Show welcome page on startup at the bottom of Welcome. Status bar at the very bottom (errors, warnings, account, Live Share). Open the project folder Create a folder named 30DaysOfPython on your desktop. In Explorer, click Open Folder. The empty state says You have not yet opened a folder. In the file dialog, go to Desktop and select the 30DaysOfPython folder. Click Open. (The dialog also has Cancel and New Folder.) Create the first file After the folder is open, Explorer shows shortcuts on the 30DAYSOF... row: Click the New File icon (page with a plus) to create a file. Click the New Folder icon (folder with a plus) to create a folder. Name the file helloworld.py. A Python file always uses the .py extension. Click the Explorer icon on the activity bar to show or hide the file tree. Close the opened project Right-click the 30DaysOfPython folder name in Explorer (not the file). The menu includes: New File, New Folder, Reveal in Finder, Open in Terminal, Add Folder to Workspace, Open Folder Settings, Remove Folder from Workspace, Find in Folder, Paste, Copy Path, Copy Relative Path, Generate .editorconfig, Deploy to Web App. Choose Remove Folder from Workspace. The development environment is ready. Next we write Python. Basic Python Python Syntax A Python script can be written in the Python interactive shell or in the code editor. A Python file has an extension .py. Python Indentation An indentation is a white space in a text. Indentation in many languages is used to increase code readability; however, Python uses indentation to create blocks of code. In other programming languages, curly brackets are used to create code blocks instead of indentation. One of the common bugs when writing Python code is incorrect indentation. A line that starts with extra space before any block is an error. example.py "Hello, World!" # This will cause an indentation error "Hello, World!" # This will run without causing error View: output.txt >>> "Hello, World!" # This will cause an indentation error File "", line 1 "Hello, World!" # This will cause an indentation error IndentationError: unexpected indent >>> "Hello, World!" # This will run without causing error 'Hello, World!' Do not put spaces in front of a top-level line. You will use indentation on purpose later, inside if and loops. Comments Comments play a crucial role in enhancing code readability and allowing developers to leave notes within their code. In Python, any text preceded by a hash (#) symbol is considered a comment and is not executed when the code runs. Example: Single Line Comment example.py # This is the first comment # This is the second comment # Python is eating the world Example: Multiline Comment A triple quote can be used for a multiline comment if it is not assigned to a variable. example.py """This is multiline comment multiline comment takes multiple lines. python is eating the world """ Data types In Python there are several types of data types. Let us get started with the most common ones. Different data types will be covered in detail in other sections. For the time being, let us just go through the different data types and get familiar with them. You do not have to have a clear understanding now. Number Integer: Integer (negative, zero and positive) numbers Example: ... -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 ... Structured set we use today: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 Float: Decimal number Example: ... -3.5, -2.25, -1.0, 0.0, 1.1, 2.2, 3.5 ... Structured examples: 10.0, 3.14, 9.81 Complex Example: 1 + 1j, 2 + 4j Structured example: 1 + 3j String A collection of one or more characters under a single or double quote. If a string is more than one sentence then we use a triple quote. Example: example.py 'Priya' 'India' 'Python' 'I love teaching' 'I hope you are enjoying the first day of 30DaysOfPython Challenge' Booleans A boolean data type is either a True or False value. T and F should be always uppercase. Example: example.py True # Is the light on? If it is on, then the value is True False # Is the light on? If it is off, then the value is False List Python list is an ordered collection which allows to store different data type items. A list is similar to an array in JavaScript. Example: example.py [10, 20, 30, 40, 50] # all the same data types - a list of numbers ['Banana', 'Orange', 'Mango', 'Avocado'] # all the same data types - a list of strings (fruits) ['India', 'Finland', 'Sweden', 'Norway'] # all the same data types - a list of strings (countries) ['Banana', 10, False, 9.81] # different data types - string, integer, boolean and float Dictionary A Python dictionary object is an unordered collection of data in a key value pair format. Example: example.py { 'first_name': 'Priya', 'last_name': 'Rao', 'country': 'India', 'city': 'Hyderabad', 'age': 22, 'is_married': False, 'skills': ['JS', 'React', 'Node', 'Python'] } Tuple A tuple is an ordered collection of different data types like list but tuples can not be modified once they are created. They are immutable. Example: example.py ('Priya', 'Rao', 'Brook', 'Abraham', 'Lidiya') # Names example.py ('Earth', 'Jupiter', 'Neptune', 'Mars', 'Venus', 'Saturn', 'Uranus', 'Mercury') # planets Set A set is a collection of data types similar to list and tuple. Unlike list and tuple, set is not an ordered collection of items. Like in Mathematics, set in Python stores only unique items. In later sections, we will go in detail about each and every Python data type. Example: example.py {10, 20, 30, 40} {3.14, 9.81, 2.7} # order is not important in set Checking Data types To check the data type of certain data/variable we use the type function. example.py type(10) type(3.14) type(1 + 3j) type('Priya') type([10, 20, 30]) type({'name': 'Priya'}) type((10, 20, 30, 40)) type({9.8, 3.14, 2.7}) exit() View: output.txt >>> type(10) >>> type(3.14) >>> type(1 + 3j) >>> type('Priya') >>> type([10, 20, 30]) >>> type({'name': 'Priya'}) >>> type((10, 20, 30, 40)) >>> type({9.8, 3.14, 2.7}) >>> exit() # Value type() view 1 10 2 3.14 3 1 + 3j 4 'Priya' 5 [10, 20, 30] 6 {'name': 'Priya'} 7 (10, 20, 30, 40) 8 {9.8, 3.14, 2.7} Python File First open your project folder, 30DaysOfPython. If you don't have this folder, create a folder named 30DaysOfPython. Inside this folder, create a file called helloworld.py. Now, let's do what we did on the Python interactive shell using Visual Studio Code. The Python interactive shell was printing without using print. In a .py file you must use the built-in function print() to see a result. print() takes one or more arguments: print('argument1', 'argument2', 'argument3'). Example The file name is helloworld.py. example.py # Day 1 - 30DaysOfPython Challenge print('Hello, World!') print(10 + 20) # addition(+) print(30 - 10) # subtraction(-) print(10 * 20) # multiplication(*) print(30 / 10) # division(/) print(10 ** 2) # exponential(**) print(30 % 20) # modulus(%) print(30 // 20) # Floor division operator(//) # Checking data types print(type(10)) # Int print(type(3.14)) # Float print(type(1 + 3j)) # Complex print(type('Priya')) # String print(type([10, 20, 30])) # List print(type({'name': 'Priya'})) # Dictionary print(type({10, 20, 30})) # Set print(type((10, 20, 30))) # Tuple How to run it Open helloworld.py in the Explorer (it sits under the 30DaysOfPython folder). Click the green Run triangle at the top right of the editor, or Open the Terminal panel and type: terminal python helloworld.py View: output.txt Hello, World! 30 20 200 3.0 100 10 1 You finished the Day 1 lesson. Practice with the exercises below. Exercises Exercises: Level 1 Check the python version you are using Open the python interactive shell and do the following operations. The operands are 3 and 4. addition(+) subtraction(-) multiplication(*) modulus(%) division(/) exponential(**) floor division operator(//) Write strings on the python interactive shell. The strings are the following: Your name Your family name Your country I am enjoying 30 days of python Check the data types of the following data: 10 9.8 3.14 4 - 4j ['Asabeneh', 'Python', 'Finland'] Your name Your family name Your country Exercises: Level 2 Create a folder named day_1 inside 30DaysOfPython folder. Inside day_1 folder, create a python file helloworld.py and repeat questions 1, 2, 3 and 4. Remember to use print() when you are working on a python file. Navigate to the directory where you have saved your file, and run it. Exercises: Level 3 Write an example for different Python data types such as Number(Integer, Float, Complex), String, Boolean, List, Tuple, Set and Dictionary. Find an Euclidean distance between (2, 3) and (10, 8) Store the structured numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 in a list named scores. Use print(scores) and print(type(scores)) Use print() and type() on 10, 20.0, 10 + 20j, 'Priya', and True. Print each value and each type Print each score with a label: print('score 1:', 10) through print('score 5:', 50) Print 10 + 20, 30 - 10, 10 * 20, 30 / 10, 10 ** 2, 30 % 20, and 30 // 20. Then print type() of each result Build a dictionary for Priya Rao in Hyderabad, India, with a score of 20. Print the dictionary and type() of it Compare type([10, 20, 30]), type((10, 20, 30)), and type({10, 20, 30}). Print all three views and write one comment about the difference You finished Day 1. Next: variables and built-in functions.

html:
Built in functions

In Python we have lots of built-in functions. Built-in functions are globally available for your use that mean you can make use of the built-in functions without importing or configuring. Some of the most commonly used Python built-in functions are the following: print(), len(), type(), int(), float(), str(), input(), list(), dict(), min(), max(), sum(), sorted(), open(), file(), help(), and dir(). In the following table you will see an exhaustive list of Python built-in functions taken from python documentation.

Full list of built-in functions

Built-in Functions
abs() delattr() hash() memoryview() set()
all() dict() help() min() setattr()
any() dir() hex() next() slice()
ascii() divmod() id() object() sorted()
bin() enumerate() input() oct() staticmethod()
bool() eval() int() open() str()
breakpoint() exec() isinstance() ord() sum()
bytearray() filter() issubclass() pow() super()
bytes() float() iter() print() tuple()
callable() format() len() property() type()
chr() frozenset() list() range() vars()
classmethod() getattr() locals() repr() zip()
compile() globals() map() reversed() __import__()
complex() hasattr() max() round()

Python 3.10+ also adds aiter() and anext() for async loops. Use them later, not on Day 2.

Every function from the table is written below: what it does, the syntax, and a small view. You do not have to memorize the whole list today. The common ones (print, len, type, int, float, str, input, min, max, sum, help, dir) are practiced in the next section.

# Function What it does Example View
1 abs(x) Absolute value (no minus sign) abs(-20) 20
2 all(iterable) True if every item is true all([10, 20, 30]) True
3 any(iterable) True if at least one item is true any([0, 0, 10]) True
4 ascii(x) Text form using ASCII escape codes ascii('café') 'caf\\xe9'
5 bin(x) Integer as a binary string bin(10) '0b1010'
6 bool(x) Convert to True or False bool(0) / bool(10) False / True
7 breakpoint() Pause the program in the debugger breakpoint() debugger starts
8 bytearray(x) Changeable sequence of bytes bytearray(3) bytearray(b'\\x00\\x00\\x00')
9 bytes(x) Frozen sequence of bytes bytes(3) b'\\x00\\x00\\x00'
10 callable(x) True if you can call it like a function callable(print) True
11 chr(n) Number to one character chr(65) 'A'
12 classmethod(fn) Turn a function into a class method @classmethod used inside a class
13 compile(src, file, mode) Turn source text into code you can run compile('10 + 20', '', 'eval') code object
14 complex(real, imag) Make a complex number complex(1, 3) (1+3j)
15 delattr(obj, name) Delete an attribute from an object delattr(p, 'age') attribute gone
16 dict(...) Make a dictionary dict(name='Priya', score=20) {'name': 'Priya', 'score': 20}
17 dir(x) List names / methods on an object dir(str) list of string methods
18 divmod(a, b) Quotient and remainder together divmod(50, 20) (2, 10)
19 enumerate(seq) Pair each item with its index list(enumerate(['a', 'b'])) [(0, 'a'), (1, 'b')]
20 eval(src) Run a short expression from a string eval('10 + 20') 30
21 exec(src) Run statements from a string exec('x = 10') runs the code
22 filter(fn, seq) Keep items where fn is true list(filter(lambda n: n > 20, [10, 20, 30, 40])) [30, 40]
23 float(x) Convert to a decimal number float(10) 10.0
24 format(x, spec) Format a value as text format(20, '04d') '0020'
25 frozenset(seq) Frozen (unchangeable) set frozenset([10, 20, 20]) frozenset({10, 20})
26 getattr(obj, name) Get an attribute by name getattr('Priya', 'upper') the upper method
27 globals() Dictionary of global names globals() {...}
28 hasattr(obj, name) True if the attribute exists hasattr('Priya', 'upper') True
29 hash(x) Hash number used by sets and dicts hash(10) an integer
30 help(x) Open built-in documentation help('keywords') list of reserved words
31 hex(x) Integer as a hexadecimal string hex(10) '0xa'
32 id(x) Identity number of the object id(10) a memory id
33 input(prompt) Read a line from the user (always a string) input('Name:') 'Priya'
34 int(x) Convert to a whole number int('10') 10
35 isinstance(x, t) True if x is of type t isinstance(10, int) True
36 issubclass(a, b) True if class a is a subclass of b issubclass(bool, int) True
37 iter(x) Make an iterator iter([10, 20]) iterator
38 len(x) Number of items / characters len('Hello, World!') 13
39 list(x) Make a list list('Priya') ['P', 'r', 'i', 'y', 'a']
40 locals() Dictionary of local names locals() {...}
41 map(fn, seq) Apply a function to every item list(map(str, [10, 20, 30])) ['10', '20', '30']
42 max(x) Largest value max(20, 30, 40, 50) 50
43 memoryview(x) View the memory of bytes without copying memoryview(b'abcd') memory view
44 min(x) Smallest value min(20, 30, 40, 50) 20
45 next(it) Next item from an iterator next(iter([10, 20])) 10
46 object() Make a bare empty object object() empty object
47 oct(x) Integer as an octal string oct(10) '0o12'
48 open(file) Open a file for reading or writing open('notes.txt') file object
49 ord(ch) Character to its number ord('A') 65
50 pow(a, b) a to the power of b pow(10, 2) 100
51 print(...) Show values on the screen print('Hello, World!') Hello, World!
52 property() Make a managed attribute on a class @property used inside a class
53 range(start, stop, step) Sequence of integers list(range(10, 50, 10)) [10, 20, 30, 40]
54 repr(x) Official / debug text of a value repr('Priya') "'Priya'"
55 reversed(seq) Walk a sequence backwards list(reversed([10, 20, 30])) [30, 20, 10]
56 round(x) Round a decimal number round(10.6) 11
57 set(seq) Make a set (unique items) set([10, 20, 20, 30]) {10, 20, 30}
58 setattr(obj, name, val) Set an attribute by name setattr(p, 'age', 22) p.age is 22
59 slice(start, stop) Describe a slice [10, 20, 30, 40, 50][slice(1, 4)] [20, 30, 40]
60 sorted(seq) Return a new sorted list sorted([40, 10, 30, 20]) [10, 20, 30, 40]
61 staticmethod(fn) Turn a function into a static method @staticmethod used inside a class
62 str(x) Convert to text str(10) '10'
63 sum(seq) Add the numbers in a list sum([20, 30, 40, 50]) 140
64 super() Reach the parent class super().__init__() used inside a class
65 tuple(x) Make a tuple tuple([10, 20, 30]) (10, 20, 30)
66 type(x) Data type of a value type(10) <class 'int'>
67 vars(x) __dict__ of an object vars(p) {'age': 22, ...}
68 zip(*seqs) Pair items from several lists list(zip([10, 20], [30, 40])) [(10, 30), (20, 40)]
69 __import__(name) Import a module by string name __import__('math') the math module

Variables

Variables store data in a computer memory. Mnemonic variables are recommended to use in many programming languages. A mnemonic variable is a variable name that can be easily remembered and associated. A variable refers to a memory address in which data is stored. Number at the beginning, special character, hyphen are not allowed when naming a variable. A variable can have a short name (like x, y, z), but a more descriptive name (firstname, lastname, age, country) is highly recommended.

Python Variable Name Rules

  • A variable name must start with a letter or the underscore character
  • A variable name cannot start with a number
  • A variable name can only contain alpha-numeric characters and underscores (A-z, 0-9, and _ )
  • Variable names are case-sensitive (firstname, Firstname, FirstName and FIRSTNAME) are different variables)

Here are some example of valid variable names:

terminal
firstname
lastname
age

city
first_name
last_name
capital_city
_if # if we want to use reserved word as a variable

year2021
current_year_2021
birth_year
num1
num2

Invalid variables names

terminal
first-name
first@name
first$name
num-1
1num

We will use standard Python variable naming style which has been adopted by many Python developers. Python developers use snake case(snake_case) variable naming convention. We use underscore character after each word for a variable containing more than one word(eg. first_name, last_name, engine_rotation_speed). The example below is an example of standard naming of variables, underscore is required when the variable name is more than one word.

When we assign a certain data type to a variable, it is called variable declaration. For instance in the example below my first name is assigned to a variable first_name. Variables

Variables store data in a computer memory. Mnemonic variables are recommended to use in many programming languages. A mnemonic variable is a variable name that can be easily remembered and associated. A variable refers to a memory address in which data is stored.
Number at the beginning, special character, hyphen are not allowed when naming a variable. A variable can have a short name (like x, y, z), but a more descriptive name (firstname, lastname, age, country) is highly recommended.

Python Variable Name Rules


A variable name must start with a letter or the underscore character

A variable name cannot start with a number

A variable name can only contain alpha-numeric characters and underscores (A-z, 0-9, and _ )

Variable names are case-sensitive (firstname, Firstname, FirstName and FIRSTNAME) are different variables)


Here are some example of valid variable names:
terminal
firstname
lastname
age
country
city
first_name
last_name
capital_city
_if # if we want to use reserved word as a variable
year_2021
year2021
current_year_2021
birth_year
num1
num2


Invalid variables names
terminal
first-name
first@name
first$name
num-1
1num


We will use standard Python variable naming style which has been adopted by many Python developers. Python developers use snake case(snake_case) variable naming convention. We use underscore character after each word for a variable containing more than one word(eg. first_name, last_name, engine_rotation_speed).  The example below is an example of standard naming of variables, underscore is required when the variable name is more than one word.

When we assign a certain data type to a variable, it is called variable declaration. For instance in the example below my first name is assigned to a variable first_name. title: Day 3 — Operators
html:
Boolean

A boolean data type represents one of the two values: True or False. The use of these data types will be clear once we start using the comparison operator. The first letter T for True and F for False should be capital unlike JavaScript.

Example: Boolean Values

example.py
print(True)
print(False)

View:

output.txt
True
False

Operators

Python language supports several types of operators. In this section, we will focus on a few of them. The tables below list every operator row from this lesson.

Assignment Operators

Assignment operators are used to assign values to variables. Let us take = as an example. The equal sign in mathematics shows that two values are equal. In Python it means we are storing a value in a certain variable. We call that assignment.

The table is taken from w3schools. Every row is written here.

Operator Example Same as
= x = 5 x = 5
+= x += 3 x = x + 3
-= x -= 3 x = x - 3
*= x *= 3 x = x * 3
/= x /= 3 x = x / 3
%= x %= 3 x = x % 3
//= x //= 3 x = x // 3
**= x **= 3 x = x ** 3
&= x &= 3 x = x & 3
\|= x \|= 3 x = x \| 3
^= x ^= 3 x = x ^ 3
>>= x >>= 3 x = x >> 3
<<= x <<= 3 x = x << 3

Same operators, run with the structured number 10 (and 20 / 40 where the view is clearer). The last five operators work on the bits of the integer. You do not have to master bitwise math today. You do have to know the row exists.

example.py
x = 10
print('=', x)

x += 10
print('+=', x)

x -= 10
print('-=', x)

x *= 3
print('*=', x)

x /= 2
print('/=', x)

x = 50
x %= 20
print('%=', x)

x = 50
x //= 20
print('//=', x)

x = 10
x **= 2
print('**=', x)

x = 10
x &= 3
print('&=', x)

x = 10
x |= 3
print('|=', x)

x = 10
x ^= 3
print('^=', x)

x = 40
x >>= 2
print('>>=', x)

x = 10
x <<= 2
print('<<=', x)

View:

output.txt
= 10
+= 20
-= 10
*= 30
/= 15.0
%= 10
//= 2
**= 100
&= 2
|= 11
^= 9
>>= 10
<<= 40

/= turns x into a float (15.0). Reset x before %, //, **, and the bitwise operators, or the next line uses the leftover value.

Arithmetic Operators

  • Addition(+): a + b
  • Subtraction(-): a - b
  • Multiplication(*): a * b
  • Division(/): a / b
  • Modulus(%): a % b
  • Floor division(//): a // b
  • Exponentiation(**): a ** b
Operator Name Example
+ Addition x + y
- Subtraction x - y
* Multiplication x * y
/ Division x / y
% Modulus x % y
** Exponentiation x ** y
// Floor division x // y

Example: Integers

example.py
# Arithmetic Operations in Python
# Integers

print('Addition: ', 10 + 20)        # 30
print('Subtraction: ', 20 - 10)     # 10
print('Multiplication: ', 10 * 3)   # 30
print('Division: ', 40 / 20)        # 2.0  Division in Python gives a floating number
print('Division: ', 60 / 20)        # 3.0
print('Division: ', 50 / 20)        # 2.5
print('Division without the remainder: ', 50 // 20)   # 2
print('Division without the remainder: ', 50 // 30)   # 1
print('Modulus: ', 50 % 20)         # 10, gives the remainder
print('Exponentiation: ', 10 ** 2)  # 100  it means 10 * 10

View:

output.txt
Addition:  30
Subtraction:  10
Multiplication:  30
Division:  2.0
Division:  3.0
Division:  2.5
Division without the remainder:  2
Division without the remainder:  1
Modulus:  10
Exponentiation:  100

/ always returns a float, even when the answer is a whole number (40 / 20 is 2.0). // drops the decimal. % is the leftover.

Example: Floats

example.py
# Floating numbers
print('Floating Point Number, PI', 3.14)
print('Floating Point Number, gravity', 9.81)

View:

output.txt
Floating Point Number, PI 3.14
Floating Point Number, gravity 9.81

Example: Complex numbers

example.py
# Complex numbers
print('Complex number: ', 1 + 1j)
print('Multiplying complex numbers: ', (1 + 1j) * (1 - 1j))

View:

output.txt
Complex number:  (1+1j)
Multiplying complex numbers:  (2+0j)

(1 + 1j) * (1 - 1j) is 1 - (1j)**2 which is 1 - (-1) = 2+0j.

Let's declare a variable and assign a number data type. Single-character names are used here only to match the operator tables. Do not develop a habit of declaring such types of variables. Variable names should be mnemonic.

Example:

example.py
# Declaring the variable at the top first

a = 50  # a is a variable name and 50 is an integer data type
b = 20  # b is a variable name and 20 is an integer data type

# Arithmetic operations and assigning the result to a variable
total = a + b
diff = a - b
product = a * b
division = a / b
remainder = a % b
floor_division = a // b
exponential = a ** 2

# I should have used sum instead of total but sum is a built-in function - try to avoid overriding built-in functions
print(total)
print('a + b = ', total)
print('a - b = ', diff)
print('a * b = ', product)
print('a / b = ', division)
print('a % b = ', remainder)
print('a // b = ', floor_division)
print('a ** 2 = ', exponential)

View:

output.txt
70
a + b =  70
a - b =  30
a * b =  1000
a / b =  2.5
a % b =  10
a // b =  2
a ** 2 =  2500

The first print(total) has no label. The labeled lines are easier to read. a ** 2 is used instead of a ** b so the view stays a small structured number (2500), not 50 ** 20.

Example:

example.py
print('== Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, Division, Modulus ==')

# Declaring values and organizing them together
num_one = 30
num_two = 40

# Arithmetic operations

diff = num_two - num_one
product = num_one * num_two
div = num_two / num_one
remainder = num_two % num_one

# Printing values with label
print('total: ', total)
print('difference: ', diff)
print('product: ', product)
print('division: ', div)
print('remainder: ', remainder)

division:  1.3333333333333333
remainder:  10

Let us start connecting the dots and start making use of what we already know to calculate (area, volume, density, weight, perimeter, distance, force).

Example:

example.py
# Calculating area of a circle
radius = 10                                 # radius of a circle
area_of_circle = 3.14 * radius ** 2         # two * sign means exponent or power
print('Area of a circle:', area_of_circle)

# Calculating area of a rectangle
length = 10
width = 20
area_of_rectangle = length * width
print('Area of rectangle:', area_of_rectangle)

# Calculating a weight of an object
mass = 50
gravity = 9.81
weight = mass * gravity
print(weight, 'N')                         # Adding unit to the weight

# Calculate the density of a liquid
mass = 50      # in Kg
volume = 0.05  # in cubic meter
density = mass / volume  # 1000 Kg/m^3
print(density, 'Kg/m^3')

View:

output.txt
Area of a circle: 314.0
Area of rectangle: 200
490.5 N
1000.0 Kg/m^3

** is done before *, so 3.14 * radius ** 2 is 3.14 * (10 ** 2), not (3.14 * 10) ** 2.

Comparison Operators

In programming we compare values. We use comparison operators to compare two values. We check if a value is greater or less or equal to another value. The following table shows Python comparison operators taken from w3schools. Every row is written here.

Operator Name Example
== Equal x == y
!= Not equal x != y
> Greater than x > y
< Less than x < y
>= Greater than or equal to x >= y
<= Less than or equal to x <= y

Example: Comparison Operators

example.py
print(30 > 20)     # True, because 30 is greater than 20
print(30 >= 20)    # True, because 30 is greater than 20
print(30 < 20)     # False, because 30 is greater than 20
print(20 < 30)     # True, because 20 is less than 30
print(20 <= 30)    # True, because 20 is less than 30
print(30 == 20)    # False, because 30 is not equal to 20
print(30 != 20)    # True, because 30 is not equal to 20
print(len('Priya') == len('Rao'))          # False  5 == 3
print(len('Priya') != len('Rao'))          # True
print(len('Priya') < len('Hyderabad'))     # True   5 < 9
print(len('India') != len('Rao'))          # True   5 != 3
print(len('city') == len('Rao'))           # False  4 == 3
print(len('tomato') == len('potato'))      # True   6 == 6
print(len('python') > len('dragon'))       # False  6 > 6


# Comparing something gives either a True or False

print('True == True: ', True == True)
print('True == False: ', True == False)
print('False == False:', False == False)

View:

output.txt
True
True
False
True
True
False
True
False
True
True
True
False
True
False
True == True:  True
True == False:  False
False == False: True

== is equality. = is assignment. Mixing them up is a common first-week bug.

Identity and Membership Operators

In addition to the comparison operators above, Python uses identity operators and membership operators.

Identity operators:

Operator Description Example
is Returns true if both variables are the same object x is y
is not Returns true if both variables are not the same object x is not y

Membership operators from the original lesson prose:

Operator Description Example
in Returns True if the queried list (or string) contains a certain item (x in y) 'P' in 'Priya'
not in Returns True if the queried list (or string) does not have a certain item (x not in y) 'Z' not in 'Priya'
example.py
print('1 is 1', 1 is 1)                   # True - because the data values are the same object
print('1 is not 2', 1 is not 2)           # True - because 1 is not 2
print('P in Priya', 'P' in 'Priya')       # True - P found in the string
print('B in Priya', 'B' in 'Priya')       # False - there is no uppercase B
print('code' in 'code for all')           # True - because code for all has the word code
print('a in an:', 'a' in 'an')            # True
print('4 is 2 ** 2:', 4 is 2 ** 2)        # True
print('H in Hyderabad', 'H' in 'Hyderabad')
print('Z not in India', 'Z' not in 'India')
print(10 in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
print(60 not in [10, 20, 30, 40, 50])

View:

output.txt
1 is 1 True
1 is not 2 True
P in Priya True
B in Priya False
True
a in an: True
4 is 2 ** 2: True
H in Hyderabad True
Z not in India True
True
True

== compares values. is compares identity (the same object in memory). Prefer == for numbers and strings. Python may warn when you write 1 is 1 because small literals are an implementation detail. Membership (in / not in) works on strings, lists, and other collections.

Logical Operators

Unlike other programming languages Python uses keywords and, or and not for logical operators. Logical operators are used to combine conditional statements. Every row is written here.

Operator Description Example
and Returns True if both statements are true x < 5 and x < 10
or Returns True if one of the statements is true x < 5 or x < 4
not Reverse the result, returns False if the result is true not(x < 5 and x < 10)
example.py
print(30 > 20 and 40 > 30)  # True - because both statements are true
print(30 > 20 and 40 < 30)  # False - because the second statement is false
print(30 < 20 and 40 < 30)  # False - because both statements are false
print('True and True: ', True and True)
print(30 > 20 or 40 > 30)   # True - because both statements are true
print(30 > 20 or 40 < 30)   # True - because one of the statements is true
print(30 < 20 or 40 < 30)   # False - because both statements are false
print('True or False:', True or False)
print(not 30 > 20)     # False - because 30 > 20 is true, then not True gives False
print(not True)        # False - Negation, the not operator turns true to false
print(not False)       # True
print(not not True)    # True
print(not not False)   # False

View:

output.txt
True
False
False
True and True:  True
True
True
False
True or False: True
False
False
True
True
False

and needs both sides True. or needs one side True. not flips True to False and False to True.
